source.title: Kinematic and electromyographic effects of different execution modalities during the Nordic Hamstring Exercise

paper.citation: Bergmann J., Schmidt M., Jaitner T. Kinematic and electromyographic effects of different execution modalities during the Nordic Hamstring Exercise. Sports Biomechanics. 2026;:1-20. doi:10.1080/14763141.2026.2657898.
paper.abstract: This paper addresses the following question: How do partner fixation, rigid heel fixation, and a specialized training-device setup affect Nordic Hamstring Exercise break-point angle, segment orientation, and biceps femoris/semitendinosus activation? Participants: 42 healthy recreationally active adults, age 26.4 ± 4.0 years; 24 men and 18 women. Sport and level: Mixed recreational activity rather than elite or team-sport athletes. Design: Preregistered cross-sectional randomized-order within-subject comparison. Exposure or intervention: Three Nordic modalities: partner-held heels on a mat, rigid heel fixation on a mat, and a device combining rigid fixation, elevated/controlled kneeling height, and unrestricted patellar glide.
paper.tldr: Mean break-point angles were 74.8° ± 9.4° with partner fixation, 74.3° ± 11.1° with rigid heel fixation, and 56.0° ± 13.8° with the training device; the device differed from both alternatives, while partner and rigid fixation did not differ. All participants reached their most extended break-point knee angle in the training-device condition. Nordic execution should be documented and standardized rather than treated as one interchangeable exercise.
paper.methods: Design: Preregistered cross-sectional randomized-order within-subject comparison. Exposure or intervention: Three Nordic modalities: partner-held heels on a mat, rigid heel fixation on a mat, and a device combining rigid fixation, elevated/controlled kneeling height, and unrestricted patellar glide. Comparator: Each participant performed all three modalities. Measurements and outcomes: Knee break-point angle, thigh and shank orientation, and surface-EMG RMS and integrated EMG for biceps femoris and semitendinosus. Analysis: Friedman tests with Holm-adjusted Wilcoxon post hoc comparisons, repeated-measures correlation, effect sizes, confidence intervals, and reliability assessment.
paper.findings: Mean break-point angles were 74.8° ± 9.4° with partner fixation, 74.3° ± 11.1° with rigid heel fixation, and 56.0° ± 13.8° with the training device; the device differed from both alternatives, while partner and rigid fixation did not differ. All participants reached their most extended break-point knee angle in the training-device condition. Shank orientation was associated with break-point knee angle within participants (rrm = 0.38, 95% CI 0.18–0.55, p < 0.001), indicating that setup-dependent segment configuration contributed to the angle difference. RMS activation was higher with the device than with partner or rigid fixation for both biceps femoris and semitendinosus, while the two traditional setups did not differ. Integrated EMG was highest on average with the device, but its difference from rigid heel fixation was not statistically significant; the device exceeded partner fixation.
paper.limitations: This was an acute cross-sectional comparison, so it cannot establish long-term strength, fascicle, sprint, injury, or performance adaptations. Recreationally active adults may differ from elite athletes and collegiate American-football players in strength, familiarity, and hamstring-injury risk. Few participants reached the most injury-relevant extended knee angles, limiting competitive-sport transfer. Hamstring force was not measured directly; eccentric demand was inferred from break-point geometry and EMG. Surface EMG reflects electrical activation, not force or injury protection, and is sensitive to measurement and normalization choices. Results apply to the tested device configuration as a package; they do not isolate which feature—heel rigidity, kneeling height, knee pad, or patellar glide—produced each effect.
paper.practicalImplications: Nordic execution should be documented and standardized rather than treated as one interchangeable exercise. Stable heel resistance, controlled kneeling height, shank position, and unimpeded patellar movement can change the acute stimulus. Staff can use these factors to improve repeatability and progression, but should not claim that the specialized device prevents hamstring injury or is superior for longitudinal adaptation until those outcomes are tested directly.

Use the paper as one input to interdisciplinary judgment, not as a standalone clearance criterion or reinjury prediction rule.
